# How TT-seq / TTchem-seq processing differs {#sec-tt-seq}

TT-seq libraries look like RNA-seq libraries: stranded, paired-end, Illumina
reads of RNA fragments. But they measure something different, and that changes
several steps of the processing. This chapter goes through `RNApipe` step by
step and says what changes for TT-seq and why. The lab's TT-seq pipeline is
[**TTpipe**](https://jpflores-13.github.io/TTpipe); its
[From Reads to Results](https://jpflores-13.github.io/TTpipe/journey.html)
chapter covers the biology in more depth.

## What's different about the RNA

- **RNA-seq** sequences the whole RNA pool. It is dominated by **mature,
  spliced mRNA**, which is the balance of synthesis and decay over hours.
- **TT-seq / TTchem-seq** feeds cells **4-thiouridine (4sU)** for a short pulse
  (minutes), then biotinylates and pulls down only the labelled RNA. What you
  sequence is RNA **made during the pulse**, which is mostly **unspliced
  precursor**. TTchem-seq is a variant with a different chemistry for
  the labelling and pull-down; the reads are processed the same way.

The consequence for the data: **reads fall across the whole transcribed
region, introns included**, and often run past the end of the gene. In RNA-seq
an intronic read is mostly noise. In TT-seq it's signal: direct evidence the
gene was being transcribed.

## Step by step

| Step | RNA-seq (bagPipes RNApipe) | TT-seq (TTpipe) | Why it changes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Read QC | FastQC | FastQC (same) | |
| Trimming | Trim Galore, always | Optional (fastp), off by default | STAR soft-clips leftover adapter; TTpipe follows its source guide |
| **Quantification** | **Salmon** on the transcriptome | **None.** No pseudoaligner | Salmon only knows **mature transcripts**. Intronic reads have nowhere to go, so most of the signal would be lost ([what pseudoaligners assume](tools-landscape.qmd#pseudoaligners-lightweight-mappers)) |
| Alignment | HISAT2, for tracks and QC only | **STAR**, and it's the basis of **everything**, counts included | All numbers now come from genome alignments |
| MAPQ filter | None | Keep pairs with **MAPQ ≥ 10** | Counting from the BAM, so multi-mappers must be removed or they'd be counted in several places |
| Duplicates | Kept | **Removed** (Picard) | Pull-down libraries are often low-input and PCR-heavy; TTpipe follows the guide's setting |
| **Strand** | Used for optional tracks | **Central**: every BAM split into forward and reverse strand | Nascent transcription is often bidirectional (promoters, enhancers) and antisense; overlapping genes on opposite strands must be told apart |
| **Counting** | Salmon/tximport, **exons** via transcripts | **HTSeq-count on the whole gene body** (`--type gene`: exons **and introns**), per strand | Intronic reads are signal; counting only exons would throw most of it away |
| Isoforms | Resolved by Salmon, summed by tximport | Not resolved: **one count per gene** | A gene-body count can't tell isoforms apart |
| Tracks | `bamCoverage`, raw counts, per sample (+ merged) | `bamCoverage` with **scale factors** from merged replicates, per strand | Tracks are compared across conditions, so depth must be evened out |
| Normalisation for DE | DESeq2 size factors | DESeq2 size factors, **with a caveat** (below); optional spike-in module | |
| Statistics | (after the pipeline) DESeq2 | DESeq2, GSEA and a Sankey of the time course, inside the pipeline | TT-seq is usually a time course after a perturbation |

## The normalisation caveat

DESeq2 (and any library-size normalisation) assumes **most genes don't
change**. In steady-state RNA-seq that's usually reasonable. In TT-seq the
perturbations people study (degrading a transcription factor, inhibiting
the polymerase) can **lower transcription of almost every gene**. Library-size
normalisation then hides the global drop, because every library is scaled back
to the same total.

The fix is a **spike-in**: labelled RNA from another species (e.g. *S. pombe*
or *Drosophila*) added in a fixed amount per sample, used to set the scale.
Without one, "transcription went down" means "went down **relative to other
genes**". TTpipe states this in its QC report and has an optional,
experimental spike-in module.

## QC numbers mean different things

| Metric | Healthy RNA-seq | Healthy TT-seq |
|---|---|---|
| Reads in introns | Low (a few to ~20 %) | **High**: often the majority |
| Salmon mapping rate | 70–90 % | Not used (it would look terrible, and that's expected) |
| Duplicates | Mostly from expression; ignored | Watched: very high values point to low input / over-amplification |
| Sense % (reads on the gene's strand) | High for stranded kits | High, but **antisense signal is real biology**, so not ~100 % |
| rRNA % | Low with poly-A selection | Can matter: labelled RNA isn't poly-A selected |
| Reads past the gene end | Few | Expected (read-through transcription before termination) |

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check your understanding

1. Why can't TTpipe just use Salmon and tximport like RNApipe?
2. A colleague counts TT-seq reads with featureCounts on exons only. What do they
   lose?
3. After degrading a general transcription factor, DESeq2 says only 300 genes
   go down. Should you believe that transcription barely changed?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple"}
## Answers

1. Most TT-seq reads are from unspliced precursor RNA, including introns.
   Salmon's index contains only mature transcripts, so those reads would be
   unmapped or wrongly assigned.
2. All the intronic reads, which are most of the nascent signal. Genes are
   also weighted by how much of their length happens to be exonic.
3. Not without a spike-in. A global drop is normalised away, so DESeq2 only
   reports genes that changed **relative to the rest**.
:::
:::
